entry:
Family of hoofed mammals in the order [[Perissodactyla]], including horses, asses and zebras.
The family evolved in the [[Eocene]] epoch, more than 50 million years ago, from small, multi-toed ancestors into larger, single-toed animals. The oldest known fossils, found in North America and about 54 million years old, belong to fox-sized browsers with three toes on the hind feet and four on the front. Later species reduced their toes and developed teeth for grinding grass. Equids are hindgut fermenters. During the [[Miocene]] epoch the family diversified and acquired the horse-like body shape of modern species. All living species belong to the genus *Equus*, which originated in North America and had spread through the world by the early [[Pleistocene]] epoch. Humans domesticated the donkey about 5,000 years ago and the horse about 4,200 years ago.

Semi-annual astronomical moment with the [[Sun]] directly above the [[Equator|equator]].
Equinoxes occur twice a year, around March 20 and September 23. An equinox is the moment when the plane of Earth's equator passes through the geometric center of the Sun's disk and Earth's rotation axis is perpendicular to the Sun-Earth line. The name comes from [[Latin]] *aequinoctium*, from *aequa* (equal) and *nox* (night). Day and night are nearly but not exactly equal in length, because of the Sun's angular size, atmospheric [[Refraction|refraction]] and changing day length. Equinoxes result from Earth's [[Axial tilt|axial tilt]] of 23.5 degrees. In the Northern Hemisphere the March equinox is the vernal or spring equinox and the September equinox is the autumnal or fall equinox; the reverse applies in the Southern Hemisphere. Equinoxes alternate with [[Solstice|solstices]], and [[Leap year|leap years]] shift their dates slightly.

Genus of vascular plants known as horsetails.
Equisetum is the only living genus in the family Equisetaceae, whose members reproduce by [[Spore|spores]] rather than seeds. The oldest remains of modern species appear in the Early Jurassic. The plants have hollow, jointed, ridged stems, and their leaves are reduced to sheaths at the nodes. Most temperate species die back in winter, while most tropical species are evergreen. Plants typically grow 20–150 cm tall, and some subtropical giant horsetails reportedly grow taller. Spores are borne in cone-like strobili and dispersed by four elaters that respond to moisture. The genus is near-cosmopolitan, and some species are considered [[Weed|weeds]] or invasive. The plants are toxic because they contain thiaminase, but they have been prepared as food or folk medicine. Plants of the World Online accepts 18 species, though some researchers count 25. Silica in the stems historically made them useful for scouring and polishing.

Set of legal principles supplementing, but distinct from, the [[Common law|common law]].
Equity developed in the English Court of Chancery, which created equitable doctrines distinct from the rest of English common law. These covered much of English private law, including [[Property|property]], [[Contract|contract]], [[Tort|tort]] and restitution. They produced equitable principles such as good faith, interests such as those under [[Trust (law)|trusts]], and remedies such as [[Injunction|injunctions]]. Medieval Lord Chancellors gave relief where the rigid rules of the common law courts seemed inequitable or unconscionable. The Judicature Acts of 1873–1875 abolished the split court system in England while retaining equity as a distinct but complementary set of rules. The tradition of flexible adjudication traces to [[Aristotle]]'s concept of *epieikeia* and to Roman *aequitas*. In [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]] systems equity was integrated into legal rules, but in common law systems it became an independent body of law.

Hypothesis that inertial and gravitational [[Mass|mass]] are equivalent.
The weak form, known for centuries, holds that masses of any composition in free fall follow the same trajectories and land at identical times. [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] found that gravitation is independent of the amount of mass accelerated. [[Isaac Newton|Newton]] compared the periods of pendulums of different materials, found them identical, and inferred that gravitational and inertial mass are the same. In 1907 [[Albert Einstein|Einstein]] introduced an extended form requiring that [[Special relativity|special relativity]] also hold in free fall and that the weak form be valid everywhere. This form was a critical input for [[General relativity|general relativity]]. The strong form extends the principle to stellar objects. In 1911 Einstein used it to predict that clocks run at different rates in a gravitational potential and that light bends in a gravitational field. The MICROSCOPE satellite mission (2016–2018) tested for composition-dependent violations of the weak form to 10⁻¹⁵ precision.

Mathematical relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
An equivalence relation generalizes [[Equality (mathematics)|equality]]. It partitions a set into disjoint equivalence classes, and two elements are equivalent if and only if they belong to the same class. Reflexivity means every element is equivalent to itself. Symmetry means that if *a* is equivalent to *b*, then *b* is equivalent to *a*. Transitivity means that if *a* is equivalent to *b* and *b* to *c*, then *a* is equivalent to *c*. Examples include numerical equality, similarity and congruence of [[Triangle|triangles]], and congruence modulo *n* on the [[Integer|integers]]. The relation ≥ is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric. "Approximately equal to" is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive, so it is not an equivalence relation.

1977 American [[Horror film|horror film]] written, directed and produced by [[David Lynch]].
Lynch's feature-length debut was shot in black and white in a surrealist style, with help from the American Film Institute. It follows a man left to care for his grossly deformed child in a desolate industrial landscape. Initially drawing small audiences, it became a midnight movie and a cult film. In 2004 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for preservation in the United States National Film Registry.

Dutch [[Humanism|humanist]], theologian and philosopher.
Known as Erasmus of [[Rotterdam]], he was one of the most influential scholars of the Northern [[Renaissance]]. As a Catholic priest he applied humanist methods to texts and prepared new Latin and Greek editions of the [[New Testament]] and of the Church Fathers. His annotations influenced both the Protestant [[Reformation|Reformation]] and the Catholic Reformation. His works include *The Praise of Folly* (1511) and *On Free Will* (1524), which was written against [[Martin Luther]]'s views on predestination. He remained in the [[Catholic Church]] and sought reform from within. He promoted synergism, a traditional doctrine that [[John Calvin|Calvin]] and Luther rejected in favor of monergism, and his middle position angered partisans on both sides.

Ancient Greek polymath, geographer and chief librarian of the [[Library of Alexandria]] from around 240 BC.
Born in Cyrene and educated in [[Athens]], he is best remembered for the first known calculation of Earth's circumference. He observed that the Sun stood directly overhead at Syene on the summer solstice, while a shadow at Alexandria formed a 7.2-degree angle, and he reasoned that the circumference was about 250,000 stadia. He also calculated Earth's [[Axial tilt|axial tilt]] and coined the terms [[Geography|geography]] and geographer. He founded scientific [[Chronology|chronology]], dating the sack of [[Troy]] to 1184 BC. In mathematics he devised the [[Sieve of Eratosthenes]] for identifying [[Prime number|prime numbers]]. Devotees nicknamed him *Pentathlos*, but according to the 10th-century encyclopedia *Suda*, critics called him *Beta*, or second, because he always came second.

Capital and most populated city of the [[Kurdistan Region]] in [[Iraq]].
Erbil is the region's cultural, economic, industrial and medical hub, with a population exceeding 1.5 million including surrounding districts. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, with settlement possibly dating to the 5th millennium BC. Its ancient Citadel, on a mound, was inscribed as a [[World Heritage Site]] in July 2014. The earliest historical reference, from the Third Dynasty of [[Ur]], records King Shulgi mentioning a city called Urbilum. The city came under [[Assyria|Assyrian]] control in the late 2nd millennium BC and was later part of successive empires, including the [[Achaemenid Empire]], Seleucid, Parthian and Sasanian. In the Middle Ages it was ruled by the Seljuk and [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] empires. Its archaeological museum holds a large collection of pre-Islamic art, particularly from [[Mesopotamia]].

[[Lanthanide]] [[Chemical element|chemical element]] with symbol Er and [[Atomic number|atomic number]] 68.
When isolated, erbium is a silvery-white solid metal, but in nature it is always combined with other elements. Carl Gustav Mosander discovered it in 1843 in yttrium from the Ytterby mine near Stockholm, Sweden, which gave the element its name. It is a [[Rare-earth element|rare-earth element]]. Its principal uses depend on the optical fluorescence of its pink Er³⁺ ions. Erbium-doped glass and crystals amplify signals in [[Optical fiber|optical fiber]] networks, where the 1550 nm wavelength is especially important because standard single-mode fibers have minimal loss there. In medicine, the ion's 2940 nm emission is strongly absorbed by water, making erbium [[Laser|lasers]] useful in [[Dermatology|dermatology]] and [[Dentistry|dentistry]] because their effect is superficial.

Male sexual dysfunction involving the recurring inability to achieve or maintain an erection.
Also called impotence, it is the most common sexual problem in males and can cause psychological distress. Notable predictors include aging, [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]], [[Diabetes|diabetes]], high blood pressure, [[Obesity|obesity]], smoking and [[Depression (mood)|depression]]. It is reported in 18% of males aged 50 to 59 years and 37% of males aged 70 to 75. Treatment often uses PDE5 inhibitors such as [[Sildenafil]], which dilate blood vessels to increase blood flow into the penis.

Highest level of professional [[Association football|football]] in the Netherlands.
Founded in 1956, the league has 18 clubs that each play the others twice a season. The two bottom clubs are relegated to the Eerste Divisie. The champion wins the Dutch national championship; [[AFC Ajax|Ajax]] have won the most titles, 36, and Feyenoord have won 16. In 2012 [[Rupert Murdoch]] secured the rights to the league for 12 years at a cost of €1 billion. The league was abandoned in 2020 because of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].

Group of about 50 species of [[Fungus|fungi]] in the genus *Claviceps*, mostly tropical.
The best-known member, *Claviceps purpurea*, infects [[Rye|rye]] and related grasses, replacing grain with dark sclerotia that contain toxic alkaloids. Eating contaminated grain causes ergotism in humans and other mammals. Ergot alkaloids are used to treat acute migraine, and a semi-synthetic derivative prevents postpartum hemorrhage. Lysergic acid from ergot was the precursor of [[LSD]], first synthesized in 1938.

French former footballer and actor.
Cantona played for [[Marseille]], Leeds United and Manchester United, winning four [[Premier League]] titles in five years with Manchester United. Manchester United fans called him "King Eric". He scored 20 goals in 45 matches for France. His career was marked by a poor disciplinary record, including a 1995 conviction for assault on a spectator and a suspension from football. He retired in 1997 and later acted in films including *Elizabeth* (1998) and *The Killer* (2024).

English [[Rock music|rock]] and [[Blues|blues]] guitarist, singer and songwriter.
Clapton played with the Yardbirds, John Mayall & the Bluesbreakers, Cream and Derek and the Dominos. With Derek and the Dominos he recorded *Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs*. He has sold 100 million records worldwide as a solo artist. He is the only three-time inductee to the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]. In 1998 he founded the Crossroads Centre on [[Antigua]], a medical facility for people recovering from substance abuse.

American pair responsible for the [[Columbine High School massacre]].
The two killed students and a teacher on April 20, 1999, and then died by suicide. At the time it was the deadliest high school shooting in U.S. history. Early reports described them as bullied outcasts, but many peers disputed this. Its motive remains inconclusive; proposed causes include bullying, mental illness and racism. The FBI concluded in 2000 that Harris showed psychopathic traits and Klebold an angry, depressive attitude; these conclusions have been criticized because neither had been diagnosed.

British historian and life-long Marxist.
Born in [[Alexandria]], Egypt, Hobsbawm spent his childhood mainly in [[Vienna]] and [[Berlin]] and moved to London after the rise of [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]]. After serving in the Second World War, he earned a PhD in history at the [[University of Cambridge]]. His best-known works are a tetralogy on the "long 19th century", from *The Age of Revolution* to *The Age of Empire*, and *The Age of Extremes* on the "short 20th century". In 1994 he said that the deaths of 15–20 million people under Stalin would have been worthwhile had the USSR achieved a [[Socialism|socialist]] utopia; critics argue that such remarks downplay Soviet repression.

Family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] known as the heath or heather family.
Members are most common in acidic, infertile [[Soil|soils]]. The family is large, ranking as the 14th most speciose family of flowering plants. Many members are woody shrubs or small trees with simple, often leathery, evergreen leaves.Notable members include the [[Cranberry|cranberry]], [[Blueberry|blueberry]], huckleberry, [[Rhododendron]] (including [[Azalea|azaleas]]), and heaths and heathers such as *Erica* and *Calluna*. They dominate habitats such as moors, [[Bog|bogs]] and cloud forests, particularly at elevations from 1,000 to 3,500 meters in the tropics, and many species form symbiotic relationships with mycorrhizal fungi that aid nutrient uptake. In cultivation, many species are grown for horticultural and food purposes.

German communist politician and leader of [[East Germany]], 1971–1989.
As security secretary of the Socialist Unity Party's Central Committee, Honecker was the prime organizer of the construction of the [[Berlin Wall]] in 1961, and he bore administrative responsibility for the "order to fire" along it. In 1970 he initiated a power struggle that led, with Soviet support, to his replacing Walter Ulbricht as party leader. He was viewed as a dictator. His government normalized relations with [[West Germany]] and pursued "consumer socialism" in close ties with the [[Soviet Union]]. As the [[Cold War]] eased under [[Mikhail Gorbachev]], Honecker refused all but cosmetic changes, and the party dismissed him in October 1989. After [[German reunification]] he was extradited to Germany, but the trial was abandoned because he had terminal liver cancer, and he died in exile in [[Chile]].

Prussian-born German general and politician.
In World War I he won fame for his central role in the German victories at Liège and Tannenberg in 1914. After his appointment as First Quartermaster General in 1916, he directed Germany's entire military strategy and war effort alongside [[Paul von Hindenburg]] until the country's defeat in 1918. Afterward he promoted the stab-in-the-back myth, which blamed the defeat on a treasonous conspiracy by Marxists, Freemasons and Jews. He took part in the failed 1920 Kapp Putsch and in [[Adolf Hitler|Hitler]]'s 1923 [[Beer Hall Putsch]], which contributed significantly to Hitler's rise to power. He later stood unsuccessfully for president during the [[Weimar Republic]] and wrote on military theory in *The Total War*. After his death in [[Munich]] he was given, against his explicit wishes, a state funeral organized and attended by Hitler.

Waterway in upstate New York, U.S., between the [[Hudson River]] and [[Lake Erie]].
Completed in 1825, it was the first navigable waterway connecting the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the upper [[Great Lakes]] above [[Niagara Falls]]. It sharply reduced the cost of transporting people and goods across the Appalachians, accelerated settlement of the Great Lakes region and gave New York City a strong advantage over other U.S. ports. Opponents called it "Clinton's Folly." Its construction was a landmark [[Civil engineering|civil engineering]] achievement; at 363 miles (584 km) long, it was the second-longest canal in the world after the [[Grand Canal (China)|Grand Canal]] in China. Commercial traffic declined in the 20th century, and today the canal is used mainly by recreational boats, with many [[Cycling|cyclists]] following its trail.

German-American [[Developmental psychology|developmental psychologist]] and psychoanalyst.
He formulated a theory of eight stages of psychosocial development across the human lifespan, each defined by a crisis, such as trust versus mistrust in infancy and identity versus role confusion in adolescence. He coined the phrase [[Identity (social science)|identity crisis]]. He trained in [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalysis]] in Vienna under [[Anna Freud]] and fled Nazi Germany in 1933 to settle in [[Boston]]. Despite lacking a university degree, he taught at Harvard, the [[University of California, Berkeley]] and Yale. His later works applied psychohistorical analysis to [[Martin Luther]] and [[Mahatma Gandhi]]. A 2002 survey in *Review of General Psychology* ranked him the 12th most eminent psychologist of the 20th century.

American businessman and founder of private military contractor Blackwater.
He was Blackwater's chief executive until 2009 and its chairman until its sale in 2010. In 2007 Blackwater guards killed 17 Iraqi civilians in [[Baghdad]]'s Nisour Square; four convicted guards were pardoned in 2020. Prince founded the private equity firm Frontier Resource Group in 2012 and chaired the Hong Kong-listed Frontier Services Group until 2021. He is the brother of former U.S. secretary of education Betsy DeVos.

American sportscaster and television personality.
Andrews joined [[ESPN]] in 2004 and moved to Fox Sports in 2012, where she became lead sideline reporter for the National Football League broadcasts. She placed third on the tenth season of ABC's *Dancing with the Stars* in 2010 and co-hosted the program from 2014 to 2019. She has since co-hosted *99 to Beat*, beginning in 2025.
